nodes.label: F13 eighty per cent of every swap fee is diverted to the protocol treasury
nodes.text: eighty per cent of every swap fee is diverted to the protocol treasury and twenty per cent is retained by liquidity providers
nodes.evidence: https://ethereum-rpc.publicnode.com (eth_call reserveFeePercent() = 80 on marketFactory 0x6d247b1c044fA1E22e6B04fA9F71Baf99EB29A9f, latest block, accessed 2026-08-04)
nodes.note: CANDIDATE-REGISTER (Fd). Promoted from a corpus marker into the construction: the split of realised fees between a claimant class and the treasury is what Fd names. The corpus's justification for Fd — routing to vePENDLE lockers — is stale; the route is now treasury buybacks on 14-day epochs.

nodes.label: F14 five per cent of all interest and all reward tokens accruing to yield
nodes.text: five per cent of all interest and all reward tokens accruing to yield claims is taken as a protocol fee, each leg capped in code at twenty per cent
nodes.note: CANDIDATE-REGISTER (Fd), approximate. Fd names distribution of surplus; this is a take-rate levied on another claim's accrual before the claimant sees it. Live values read 2026-08-04: interestFeeRate = rewardFeeRate = 5e16 on 0x3E6EBa46AbC5ab18ED95F6667d8B2fd4020E4637.

nodes.label: F15 anyone may create a new maturity, constrained only to a fixed 24-hour
nodes.text: anyone may create a new maturity, constrained only to a fixed 24-hour calendar grid, and anyone may create additional markets on an existing principal claim that differ only in curve parameters
nodes.note: RESIDUE. Ft names one dated claim. Pendle's object is a permissionlessly populated GRID of maturities with a birth-and-death lifecycle, each carrying unlimited parallel markets keyed by (PT, scalarRoot, initialAnchor, lnFeeRateRoot). No symbol names a term structure as an object, nor the rollover at which a maturity dies and liquidity must migrate.

nodes.label: F16 protocol tokens are issued to each market's gauge at a per-second rate
nodes.text: protocol tokens are issued to each market's gauge at a per-second rate and streamed to that market's liquidity providers

nodes.label: F17 a protocol-token holder stakes one-for-one and exits by starting a coo
nodes.text: a protocol-token holder stakes one-for-one and exits by starting a cooldown and finalising it after a fixed duration
nodes.note: APPROXIMATE. Wq names an exit queue with an ordering; sPENDLE's cooldown is a per-user delay with no ordering and no shared capacity. MAJOR DEPARTURE from the corpus: the corpus emits Ve for Pendle on contested-register grounds. As of commit e8c2cca (2026-06-17) vePendle, votingController, feeDistributor and feeDistributorV2 all sit in the repo's own `deprecated` block of deployments/1-core.json, and the replacement sPENDLE contains no escrow, no lock-weighting and no gauge vote. Ve is not among the 58 in any case; a decomposition emitting it would be decomposing a retired subsystem.

nodes.label: F18 a staker may instead exit immediately by paying a percentage of the st
nodes.text: a staker may instead exit immediately by paying a percentage of the staked amount, at a rate the owner may set up to one hundred per cent
nodes.note: RESIDUE. Wq has no room for a priced option to jump the queue. This cooldown-or-pay-to-skip pattern is new in the lane and it is what replaced a vote-escrow.

nodes.label: F19 the yield claim accrues off-chain-attested, non-token reward streams f
nodes.text: the yield claim accrues off-chain-attested, non-token reward streams from the source protocol, and the same five per cent protocol fee is levied on them
nodes.note: RESIDUE. Em requires a protocol-funded token emission. Nothing in the vocabulary names a claim on a third-party issuer's discretionary future distribution, still less a protocol taxing one.

nodes.label: F20 the yield-contract factory, market factory and governance proxy sit be
nodes.text: the yield-contract factory, market factory and governance proxy sit behind upgradeable proxies whose administrators are multisigs, and a guardian role may pause an enumerated list of addresses
nodes.note: Tg is deliberately NOT emitted: stage 1 found no timelock — getMinDelay(), delay() and MINIMUM_DELAY() all revert on the governance Safe, the governance proxy and the ProxyAdmin, and no timelock appears in the mainnet manifest. L15 (Up implies Tg or a bounded emergency process) is therefore carried only by the guardian pause. X9 does not arm: control is a 3-of-N Safe, not a single key. vePENDLE itself is not proxied (implementation slot zero) and is immutable.

nodes.label: F21 execution authority over privileged functions is granted per (caller,
nodes.text: execution authority over privileged functions is granted per (caller, function selector, target) triple rather than per role or per contract
nodes.note: RESIDUE. Au was considered and rejected: L17 requires bounded scope + revocation + expiry + nonce/domain separation, which describes a session key over the principal's own assets. hasScopedAccess[caller][selector][target] has no expiry and no nonce and operates over protocol contracts. Aw names a participation gate, not a per-selector authority lattice.

nodes.label: Spark Savings (sUSDS / Sky Savings Rate)
F1 a depositor exchanges the stablecoin for a share token whose nominal b
nodes.text: a depositor exchanges the stablecoin for a share token whose nominal balance never changes and whose redemption value rises

nodes.label: F2 interest compounds per second into a stored rate accumulator, advanced
nodes.text: interest compounds per second into a stored rate accumulator, advanced by a permissionless call and extrapolated exactly in view functions without writing state
nodes.note: Sr is approximate: this is per-second compounding of an accumulator (chi = _rpow(ssr, now - rho) * chi / RAY), not the streaming of a claim to a named recipient. Live 2026-08-04: chi = 1.105245252046483725540827799, totalAssets = 4,750,051,555.68 USDS.

nodes.label: F3 the interest owed is funded by minting internal protocol debt against
nodes.text: the interest owed is funded by minting internal protocol debt against the system's surplus/deficit account, unconditionally, with no read of revenue, reserves or any solvency condition
nodes.note: RESIDUE, and the mechanism is now named precisely: vat.suck(vow, this, diff*RAY) then usdsJoin.exit. Not Em (no separate token, no schedule); not Sl (no loss event — the deficit is created by the payment); not As (no peg rule drives it); not Fd (Fd is surplus distribution and this can run in deficit). The corpus's residue item 'a rate that can exceed protocol revenue' is confirmed. Restate the corpus's yield-source claim as funded ex post from the surplus buffer, not ex ante from realised revenue.

nodes.label: F4 the rate paid is a written number, not derived from a utilisation curv
nodes.text: the rate paid is a written number, not derived from a utilisation curve, an auction or any market; the only bound inside the savings token is that it be non-negative
nodes.note: RESIDUE. file('ssr') requires only data >= RAY. 'set by a vote' versus 'set by utilisation' versus 'set by a curve' are three different risk objects that decompose identically in this vocabulary. Confirmed at code level; the same administered-rate object appears independently at Huma 2.0 (8% APY, monthly adjustment).

nodes.label: F5 the rate may be written only by addresses enumerated in an on-chain se
nodes.text: the rate may be written only by addresses enumerated in an on-chain set which governance may add to or remove from at any time
nodes.note: MANDATE SLOT 1 (named agent) and SLOT 5 (revocation), partial fit. Aw names the caller enumeration (buds[msg.sender] == 1) and its mutability. It does not name that what is being granted is a discretionary economic authority rather than a right to participate. Independently verified: sUSDS.wards(0x36B072ed8AFE665E3Aa6DaBa79Decbec63752b22) = 1. DEPARTURE: the corpus does not carry Aw for Spark.

nodes.label: F6 the enumerated agent chooses the value of the live savings rate at its
nodes.text: the enumerated agent chooses the value of the live savings rate at its own discretion, with no objective function, trigger, target or derivation anywhere in the code
nodes.note: RESIDUE — the headline of this lane, in its rate-setting form. Tg is wrong (the change is immediate). Au is wrong (L17 wants bounded scope + revocation + expiry + nonce/domain separation, i.e. a session key over the principal's own assets; a facilitator has no expiry, no nonce, and acts over the whole system's economics). Gp names the halt but not the authority it halts. The corpus's phrase 'set by a governance vote' is superseded: governance writes the bounds, a whitelisted facilitator writes the number inside them.

nodes.label: F7 the agent may write only parameters drawn from an enumerated set of ra
nodes.text: the agent may write only parameters drawn from an enumerated set of rate identifiers, each with its own configuration record
nodes.note: MANDATE SLOT 2 (domain whitelist). RESIDUE. Live ids include 'SSR', 'DSR' and per-ilk stability fees. No symbol names a restriction of a delegated decision to a domain.

nodes.label: F8 the value written must lie between a governance-set floor and ceiling,
nodes.text: the value written must lie between a governance-set floor and ceiling, live two per cent and thirty per cent
nodes.evidence: https://ethereum-rpc.publicnode.com (eth_call cfgs('SSR') = {min 200, max 3000, step 400} on 0x36B072ed8AFE665E3Aa6DaBa79Decbec63752b22, accessed 2026-08-04)
nodes.note: MANDATE SLOT 3 (magnitude cap). RESIDUE. A numeric domain restriction on a delegated decision has no symbol; Ct is a solvency test, not a parameter envelope.

nodes.label: F9 a single update may move the rate by at most a governance-set step, li
nodes.text: a single update may move the rate by at most a governance-set step, live four percentage points, and no update may occur within a cooldown of the previous one, live sixteen hours; the update then takes effect immediately
nodes.note: MANDATE SLOT 4 (rate-of-change limit). RESIDUE. Note precisely what tau is: a cooldown SINCE the last change, not a delay BEFORE execution. Tg is therefore the wrong symbol twice over — the agent's change is immediate and does not pass the 48-hour governance pause that gates governance's own actions. Ep is wrong: there are no periods.

nodes.label: F10 the rate-setting module can be halted outright by an emergency contrac
nodes.text: the rate-setting module can be halted outright by an emergency contract, after which no agent may write anything
nodes.note: MANDATE SLOT 5 (halt). Gp names the kill switch (bad != 0) but not the mandate it kills. A sibling module in the same ecosystem (pau-administered-agent) deliberately separates grantors from revokers so that revokers act as live watchdogs; Tg, Gp and Au all treat authority as a single scalar and cannot express that split.

nodes.label: F11 governance's own parameter changes execute only after a forty-eight-ho
nodes.text: governance's own parameter changes execute only after a forty-eight-hour delay

nodes.label: F12 a holder may redeem the share for the underlying stablecoin at the cur
nodes.text: a holder may redeem the share for the underlying stablecoin at the current accumulator value at any time
nodes.note: Large mainnet withdrawals are routed through an off-chain 'Savings Liquidity Intents' request fulfilled within minutes; that routing is a service level, not a contract term, and is not decomposed.

nodes.label: F13 the underlying stablecoin swaps one-for-one against a reserve asset th
nodes.text: the underlying stablecoin swaps one-for-one against a reserve asset through a peg module at zero fee, subject to a buffer, with the fee range bounded in code
nodes.evidence: https://ethereum-rpc.publicnode.com (eth_call tin() = 0, tout() = 0, buf() = 800,000,000 on 0xf6e72Db5454dd049d0788e411b06CfAF16853042, accessed 2026-08-04)
nodes.note: INHERITED, corpus marker retained. The peg module belongs to the Sky/USDS system that the savings product sits on, not to the savings product. It is load-bearing for solvency while being invisible as a property of the thing decomposed; the vocabulary has no way to mark an element as inherited from a dependency.

nodes.label: F14 the savings claim is represented on six other chains by a token minted
nodes.text: the savings claim is represented on six other chains by a token minted and burned against the mainnet position

nodes.label: F15 the rate tuple (rate, accumulator, timestamp) is forwarded to each rem
nodes.text: the rate tuple (rate, accumulator, timestamp) is forwarded to each remote chain over that chain's canonical bridge and accepted only after application-level sanity checks including an upper bound on the rate and enforcement of event ordering
nodes.note: DEPARTURE: the corpus carries neither Xm nor Ex for Spark. Xm names the canonical-bridge verification; Ex names the remote oracle that publishes the tuple. The maxSSR bound exists explicitly to bound the damage of a compromised bridge, which is L13-shaped freshness/validity validation.

nodes.label: F16 the remote token contains no accrual state and no drip function at all
nodes.text: the remote token contains no accrual state and no drip function at all; its value is extrapolated locally from the forwarded tuple and its redeemability is limited by local peg-module inventory rather than by the mainnet balance sheet
nodes.note: RESIDUE, and the corpus's version of this item is materially wrong rather than merely incomplete. The corpus assumed cross-chain sameness was economic identity; it is not. The mainnet claim can mint against the system's deficit account, the remote claim cannot. The unnamed object is a replicated index with a locally-bounded settlement guarantee. A construction that models the eight chains as one claim gets the failure modes wrong.

nodes.label: F17 the system's own capital — not the depositor's claim — is deployed int
nodes.text: the system's own capital — not the depositor's claim — is deployed into external protocols by a named multisig role, with custody of all deployed funds sitting in a single proxy
nodes.note: MANDATE SLOT 1 (named agent), partial fit, second instance at this application. SCOPE: obligations F17-F20 belong to the Spark Liquidity Layer, which DefiLlama files as a separate protocol in a separate category (Onchain Capital Allocator, $1.58bn). They are included because the newer Spark Savings vaults are documented as generating yield 'via the Spark Liquidity Layer', and because the same organisation shipping the claim and the mandate as different objects with different addresses is itself the evidence for a missing level. Verified: MainnetController.hasRole(RELAYER, 0x8a25A24EDE9482C4Fc0738F99611BE58F1c839AB) = 1.

nodes.label: F18 that role may act only through an enumerated set of twenty-nine venue-
nodes.text: that role may act only through an enumerated set of twenty-nine venue-specific actions — mint, swap, deposit into a named vault, subscribe to a named fund, bridge by a named route — and cannot construct a new one
nodes.note: MANDATE SLOT 2 (domain whitelist). RESIDUE. Governance determines the use cases supported; the numeric value of each limit is UNKNOWN (the docs defer to Sky Atlas and per-key live values were not read).

nodes.label: F19 each enumerated action carries a maximum amount and a slope that regen
nodes.text: each enumerated action carries a maximum amount and a slope that regenerates spent capacity continuously with elapsed time
nodes.note: MANDATE SLOTS 3 and 4 fused (magnitude cap plus rate-of-change limit) into one leaky bucket: _min(slope * (now - lastUpdated) + lastAmount, maxAmount). RESIDUE. Not Ep (no discrete periods), not Wq (no ordering, no queue), not Ct (no solvency test). A continuously regenerating throughput allowance on an agent has no symbol, and it is the closest thing in the lane to a general form of the mandate envelope.

nodes.label: F20 a separate multisig can freeze the controller without being able to us
nodes.text: a separate multisig can freeze the controller without being able to use it
nodes.note: MANDATE SLOT 5 (halt). Gp names the freeze. It does not name that the right to halt is deliberately held by a different party from the right to act, which is the whole accountability design.

nodes.label: F21 the savings token itself sits behind an upgradeable proxy whose admini
nodes.text: the savings token itself sits behind an upgradeable proxy whose administrator is the governance pause proxy
nodes.note: L15 is satisfied here: the upgrade path runs through the 48-hour pause proxy (F11). Not an obligation but a measurement hazard for stage 6: live sUSDS.totalAssets() = $4.750bn against DefiLlama's Spark Savings line of $1,132,142,962.30, so a paper figure must state which of the two it means.

nodes.label: 07-bridges
Binance Bitcoin (BTCB)
F1 A holder deposits bitcoin to Binance.com, where it becomes an exchange
nodes.text: A holder deposits bitcoin to Binance.com, where it becomes an exchange account balance, and then withdraws 'BTC' over the BSC network; what arrives is BTCB, an 18-decimal BEP-20 at 0x7130d2a12b9bcbfae4f2634d864a1ee1ce3ead9c, of which 65,300.96996478 is outstanding.
nodes.note: APPROXIMATE, and the weakest instance of Xf in the project. There is no source-domain event at all: the debit is a row in an exchange's internal ledger and the credit is a transfer of tokens the owner key already minted. Law L9 (debit(source) = credit(destination)) is not merely unverified here, it is UNEVALUABLE -- one side of the equality is not an object in any domain the formalism describes. Compare WBTC, where at least the Bitcoin-side deposit is a public transaction.

nodes.label: F2 What secures the peg is Binance's statement that it holds an equivalen
nodes.text: What secures the peg is Binance's statement that it holds an equivalent amount of bitcoin in multi-signature cold storage; there is no message, no proof, no verifier and no threshold of any kind.
nodes.note: RESIDUE, category headline confirmed for the third of three custodial wrappers and without qualification: none of the three contains any verification mechanism, and for this one no verification mechanism is even constructible, because the source domain cannot execute code. VERIFICATION-MODEL AXIS: single-company attestation. Xm must not be assigned. Law L8's 'named custodian' branch again discharges Xf with something that is not an element.

nodes.label: F3 Nothing is locked in a contract on either side: the issuer describes t
nodes.text: Nothing is locked in a contract on either side: the issuer describes the mechanism as a swap in which 'their Bitcoin remains locked and can be redeemed by depositing BTCB back', with the lock being an internal custody arrangement rather than an escrow.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. SUPPLY-TOPOLOGY AXIS: custodial wrap settled by an exchange-internal ledger entry -- a fifth topology the corpus's four do not include, since even 'custodial wrap' presumes a deposit address the user sends to. Nothing names an exchange ledger as the settlement layer of a bridge.

nodes.label: F4 Redemption is depositing BTCB back to Binance and withdrawing BTC over
nodes.text: Redemption is depositing BTCB back to Binance and withdrawing BTC over the Bitcoin network.
nodes.note: APPROXIMATE, the same overstatement as WBTC F7 and Coinbase F5: redemption is an exchange withdrawal subject to account standing, KYC tier, network status and unilateral suspension, not a contract-enforced right. Rd asserts the right and cannot state its conditions or who may exercise it.

nodes.label: F5 Access to both mint and redemption runs through an exchange account, s
nodes.text: Access to both mint and redemption runs through an exchange account, so only KYC'd customers in eligible jurisdictions can enter or exit, and the exchange can freeze an account and refuse redemption with no on-chain action whatsoever.
nodes.note: RESIDUE, and two CORPUS DEPARTURES. Aw is dropped: there is no on-chain permission or identity gate of any kind, and the gate that exists is enforced inside a company and is unobservable and unfalsifiable on chain. Fz is dropped: 'issuer can freeze' is false on-chain -- no blacklist, no forced transfer -- and true at the account layer, which is invisible to the token. Both powers are real and neither is nameable, which is a sharper failure than either being absent.

nodes.label: F6 Issuance is unbounded and unilateral: mint(uint256) is onlyOwner, owne
nodes.text: Issuance is unbounded and unilateral: mint(uint256) is onlyOwner, owner() = getOwner() = 0xf68a4b64162906eff0ff6ae34e2bb1cd42fef62d, and eth_getCode on that address returns empty, so a single externally-owned account can mint arbitrarily against a multi-billion-dollar liability.
nodes.evidence: https://bsc-rpc.publicnode.com eth_call owner(), getOwner() and eth_getCode(owner), empty (accessed 2026-08-04) | https://bscscan.com/address/0x7130d2a12b9bcbfae4f2634d864a1ee1ce3ead9c#code (accessed 2026-08-04)
nodes.note: RESIDUE. Aw was considered and rejected: reading onlyOwner as a permission gate would make Aw true of every ownable contract ever deployed and drain the symbol, which is precisely the objection the corpus itself raises against Xm. The control-and-authority group has no symbol whose weakest reading is this weak, and it has no way at all to record that an issuance power is unbounded in size.

nodes.label: F7 The on-chain artefact of a redemption is a self-burn -- burn(uint256)
nodes.text: The on-chain artefact of a redemption is a self-burn -- burn(uint256) burns the caller's own balance -- with nothing in the transaction linking it to a bitcoin payout or to a redeeming party.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. Contrast WBTC, where burn() runs through a Factory that records the merchant, the request and the destination address. Here the burn and the redemption are two unlinked events, so even the redemption leg cannot be audited on chain.

nodes.label: F8 The entire on-chain governance surface is transferOwnership and renoun
nodes.text: The entire on-chain governance surface is transferOwnership and renounceOwnership: the contract is Binance's standard BEP20Token template (solc 0.5.16, Apache-2.0, verified Exact Match, not a proxy) with no pause, no blacklist, no forced transfer, no upgrade path, no timelock, no multisig and no registry.
nodes.note: CORPUS DEPARTURE: Gp is dropped. The corpus gives BTCB an emergency guardian or pause and the contract HAS NO PAUSE FUNCTION -- the verified source and function list show mint, burn, transfer, approve, owner, transferOwnership and renounceOwnership and nothing else. Whatever emergency power the issuer has is exercised at the exchange, not on the token. Dropping Gp here is what breaks the corpus's claim that the three custodial wrappers decompose identically in the control plane.

nodes.label: F9 The authority over that surface is one key: not a quorum, not a contra
nodes.text: The authority over that surface is one key: not a quorum, not a contract, not a delay, with no published internal process binding its use.
nodes.note: RESIDUE, and the reason the category's control-plane ordering inverts. The vocabulary names facilities (Tg, Up, Gp) and not holders, so it cannot rank one EOA with unlimited mint (here) against two independent multisig quorums with pause only (WBTC) against single EOAs holding upgrade and freeze (Coinbase). On the corpus's arrays BTCB is a proper subset of the other two and therefore reads as the mildest of the three; on the evidence it has by a wide margin the weakest control plane in the category.

nodes.label: F10 The issuer publishes a Proof of Collateral page for its pegged tokens
nodes.text: The issuer publishes a Proof of Collateral page for its pegged tokens reporting BTC at 100%, with Proof of Assets of 68,200 BTC at a single published bitcoin address, against wrapped supplies of 2,900 on Ethereum, 128 on BEP2 and 65,222 on BEP20, plus Pioneer Burn 24 BTC and Token Recovered 49 BTC, covering 97 tokens.
nodes.note: APPROXIMATE against law L27 (At -> named attester + independence + stated assurance + staleness bound + recourse): none of the five holds. It is a self-published address listing with no auditor and no recourse. RANKING BASIS, MIS-ATTRIBUTED: DefiLlama binance-bitcoin = $4,371,846,939 against the corpus's $4,363.3m, but it tracks the 68,200 BTC in this Proof-of-Assets address -- the reserve for ALL Binance-Peg BTC across BEP20, BEP2 and Ethereum -- and not the 65,301 BTCB on BNB Chain that is the token being decomposed (about $4.20b at the same price). Rank #5 stands; the figure measures a wider liability set than the named token. WITHDRAWN: L27 requires of At a named attester, independence, a stated assurance level, a staleness bound and recourse. The cited disclosure is published by the issuer and supplies none of the last four, so At is not discharged and this obligation is residue.

nodes.label: F11 The issuer discloses that the peg may not hold exactly: 'the amount of
nodes.text: The issuer discloses that the peg may not hold exactly: 'the amount of locked BTC may not be precisely the same as the wrapped BTC due to the delays caused by the extensive auditing process', with no bound stated on the discrepancy.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. At cannot express 'we publish an address, and by the way the numbers may not match, and we do not say by how much'. A disclosed but unbounded tolerance is a term of the instrument, and the vocabulary treats a reserve claim as binary.

nodes.label: F12 One reserve pool is drawn against by three pegged representations of t
nodes.text: One reserve pool is drawn against by three pegged representations of the same asset on three different ledgers -- Ethereum, BEP2 and BEP20 -- so no single representation's backing is separable.
nodes.note: RESIDUE, the same shape as Coinbase F18 and unnamed for the same reason. Prohibition X8 ('shared collateral across nominally isolated markets') is the nearest rule in the algebra and is written for lending markets; the pattern here is identical and the rule cannot reach it.

nodes.label: F13 Two reserve claims exist over the same custodian and must not be added
nodes.text: Two reserve claims exist over the same custodian and must not be added together: 68,200 BTC of pegged-token collateral on the Proof of Collateral page, and 640,780.255 BTC of exchange customer reserve on the Proof of Reserves page (monthly Merkle-tree and zk-SNARK snapshot, latest 01/07/26 00:00 UTC at BTC block 956,140, ratio 100.08%), the first page carrying an explicit disclaimer that it is not the exchange's proof of reserve.
nodes.note: RESIDUE, and the sharpest At finding in the category. Nothing names the risk that the two claims are the same coins. Worse: the two regimes are epistemically miles apart -- one is a self-published address list, the other a monthly zk-proven liability attestation -- and At is the only symbol available for either, so a decomposition that used At for both would assert they are the same kind of object. The zk attestation covers customer liabilities and says nothing about BTCB, so it is not part of this construction.

nodes.label: F14 No independent auditor attests to the BTCB collateral specifically; no
nodes.text: No independent auditor attests to the BTCB collateral specifically; no such report was found.
nodes.note: RESIDUE, and flagged UNKNOWN by stage 1 rather than asserted as absence: the finding is that no attestation could be located, not that none exists. Recorded because At was assigned on the strength of F10 and a reader will otherwise assume an attester stands behind it. There is also no specification, no whitepaper describing the mechanism, no audit and no public source repository -- the canonical artefact is the verified contract itself.

nodes.label: F15 A holder's transfers cannot be blocked and a holder's balance cannot b
nodes.text: A holder's transfers cannot be blocked and a holder's balance cannot be seized on-chain: the token has no freeze, no blacklist and no forced-transfer function.
nodes.note: RESIDUE of the guarantee-by-absence kind, and it cuts against the intuition the corpus encodes: on the one dimension a holder can actually check, the weakest-governed of the three custodial wrappers gives the strongest guarantee, because there is no code to do anything with. The vocabulary can only express this by omitting Fz, which is indistinguishable from not having looked.

nodes.id: protocol:Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets)
nodes.label: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets)
nodes.local_id: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets)

nodes.id: obligation:Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F1
nodes.label: F1 A customer withdrawing BTC (or DOGE, XRP, ADA, LTC, MEGA) from a Coinb
nodes.protocol: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets)
nodes.text: A customer withdrawing BTC (or DOGE, XRP, ADA, LTC, MEGA) from a Coinbase account to a supported network receives a 1:1 wrapped ERC-20 instead of the native asset: cbBTC on Base, Ethereum, Solana and Arbitrum, and cbDOGE, cbXRP, cbADA, cbLTC, cbMEGA on Base.
nodes.note: APPROXIMATE at the level of law L9 (Xf -> debit(source) = credit(destination)). The credit is a mint and is observable; the debit is a ledger entry inside a company and is not, so the law's equality has one observable side and one asserted side. Xf presumes a source-domain transaction; here there is none.
nodes.local_id: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F1

nodes.id: obligation:Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F2
nodes.label: F2 What secures the peg is that Coinbase holds the underlying asset and c
nodes.protocol: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets)
nodes.text: What secures the peg is that Coinbase holds the underlying asset and continues to unwrap on demand; there is no message, no proof, no verifier set and no threshold anywhere in the system.
nodes.note: RESIDUE, category headline confirmed for the second of three custodial wrappers. VERIFICATION-MODEL AXIS: single-company attestation, and here minting is an operational decision rather than an attested event. Xm must not be assigned. As with WBTC, law L8 discharges Xf by a 'named custodian' branch that is not an element.
nodes.local_id: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F2

nodes.id: obligation:Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F3
nodes.label: F3 No contract escrows the underlying on any source chain, and five of th
nodes.protocol: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets)
nodes.text: No contract escrows the underlying on any source chain, and five of the six source assets live on chains that cannot run a verification contract at all -- Bitcoin, XRP, Dogecoin, Cardano and Litecoin -- while the sixth, MegaETH, can.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. SUPPLY-TOPOLOGY AXIS: custodial wrap. The corpus residue says this bridges five non-smart-contract source chains; it is now five of six, cbMEGA being the exception, so the claim needs the qualifier. The vocabulary's cross-domain group assumes both domains can execute code, which is false for five sixths of this application.
nodes.local_id: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F3

nodes.id: obligation:Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F4
nodes.label: F4 The conversion is a side effect of a transfer rather than a transactio
nodes.protocol: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets)
nodes.text: The conversion is a side effect of a transfer rather than a transaction the user submits: the user asked to withdraw BTC, and the system delivered cbBTC; sending the wrapped token back to a Coinbase account auto-unwraps it.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. No element for a domain crossing that the user does not initiate and cannot decline at the point of transfer.
nodes.local_id: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F4

nodes.id: obligation:Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F5
nodes.label: F5 Redemption is depositing the wrapped token into a Coinbase account, wh
nodes.protocol: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets)
nodes.text: Redemption is depositing the wrapped token into a Coinbase account, which auto-unwraps it and credits the underlying asset; there is no contract-level redemption and no order book or trading pair for the wrapped token on Coinbase.
nodes.note: APPROXIMATE, same overstatement as WBTC F7: redemption is an account action governed by the User Agreement and gated by account standing, not a contract right, and non-customers have no redemption path at all. Rd asserts a right and cannot say who holds it or under what terms it is withdrawn.
nodes.local_id: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F5

nodes.id: obligation:Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F6
nodes.label: F6 The redemption right is conditioned on jurisdiction and asset: cbBTC c
nodes.protocol: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets)
nodes.text: The redemption right is conditioned on jurisdiction and asset: cbBTC cannot be sent or received by accounts in Canada, Japan and Georgia, and the other five wrapped assets are blocked in over a hundred jurisdictions including most of the EEA, Japan, Singapore, Hong Kong and New York State.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. Rd cannot carry a jurisdiction vector and Aw gates access, not redemption. Law L26 (Aw + Xf -> destination-enforced eligibility + revocation propagation + jurisdictional binding) is the nearest rule and points the wrong way: it demands enforcement at the destination, whereas this eligibility is enforced at the issuer's account layer, invisible to every contract in the construction. The same token has a redemption right in one country and not in another.
nodes.local_id: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F6

nodes.id: obligation:Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F7
nodes.label: F7 The issuer publishes a live per-address proof of reserves -- 96,065.18
nodes.protocol: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets)
nodes.text: The issuer publishes a live per-address proof of reserves -- 96,065.18 BTC of reserve against 96,054.41 cbBTC of supply, 20 reserve addresses, refreshed 8/4/2026 8:45 PM, split 48,338.78 / 44,528.809 / 3,108.551 / 78.272 across four networks -- and the Ethereum-side supply reads 48,338.77958531 cbBTC on chain, matching the first bucket exactly.
nodes.note: APPROXIMATE against law L27 (At -> named attester + independence + stated assurance + staleness bound + recourse): there is an attester (the issuer, not independent), a timestamp, no assurance level and no recourse. CORPUS DEPARTURE: the corpus marker calls the reporting 'periodic'; it is a live per-address feed with a machine-readable JSON endpoint, plus a reported Chainlink Proof of Reserve feed on Base and Ethereum (third-party source only, chainlink social post, not a first-party Coinbase page). Still issuer-published, but 'periodic' is no longer accurate. At launch on 2024-09-12 the issuer said proof of reserves 'will follow'; it now exists, including per-asset pages for the other wrapped assets. WITHDRAWN: L27 requires of At a named attester, independence, a stated assurance level, a staleness bound and recourse. The cited disclosure is published by the issuer and supplies none of the last four, so At is not discharged and this obligation is residue.
nodes.local_id: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F7

nodes.id: obligation:Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F8
nodes.label: F8 Third parties treat the issuer's own reserve JSON as ground truth for
nodes.protocol: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets)
nodes.text: Third parties treat the issuer's own reserve JSON as ground truth for the protocol's size: DefiLlama's adapter calls getConfig('coinbase-cbbtc-proof-of-reserves', 'https://www.coinbase.com/cbbtc/proof-of-reserves.json') and sums the declared addresses.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. At names an attestation; it cannot name the circularity in which the measured value of a $6.16b protocol is the issuer's own file. RANKING BASIS: DefiLlama coinbase-bridge = $6,162,585,917 against the corpus's $6,150.9m, of which $6,158.1m (99.93%) is cbBTC -- rank #3 stands and the entry is de facto a cbBTC entry.
nodes.local_id: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F8

nodes.id: obligation:Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F9
nodes.label: F9 Issuance authority is a chain of on-chain roles: an owner appoints a m
nodes.protocol: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets)
nodes.text: Issuance authority is a chain of on-chain roles: an owner appoints a masterMinter, which grants and revokes per-minter allowances; on Ethereum owner = 0xce56d20689d836ec7a728ceb94a15746696c16e6 and masterMinter = 0x1302dfb1f806398f48650c75ab0fda9a0186f47b.
nodes.note: APPROXIMATE. Aw is a user-facing permission gate as written; here it is a registry of permitted issuers with per-party allowances -- the same issuer-side reading the corpus marks for CCTP. It is a weaker instance than WBTC's Members registry, which enumerates 47 counterparties and a custodian.
nodes.local_id: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F9

nodes.id: obligation:Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F10
nodes.label: F10 Minting is rate-limited with programmatic allowance replenishment: a M
nodes.protocol: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets)
nodes.text: Minting is rate-limited with programmatic allowance replenishment: a MintForwarder contract lets a minter continuously mint up to N tokens over M time without a cold masterMinter key having to top the allowance back up.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. A bounded issuance rate is a genuine safety mechanism -- the only quantitative bound on any authority in the three custodial wrappers -- and no element names it. The nearest shapes in the vocabulary are Wq (rationing exits) and Ep (epoch boundaries), and neither is a rate limit on a privileged action.
nodes.local_id: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F10

nodes.id: obligation:Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F11
nodes.label: F11 A named blacklister role -- 0x5130bf38bf5342aa06cc79b8cc198cce832b01af
nodes.protocol: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets)
nodes.text: A named blacklister role -- 0x5130bf38bf5342aa06cc79b8cc198cce832b01af -- can blacklist and un-blacklist any address, blocking that holder's transfers at transfer time.
nodes.note: CANDIDATE-REGISTER (Fz), and a firm assignment rather than a marker: Coinbase is the ONLY one of the three custodial wrappers with an on-chain freeze. Two elements are listed because both genuinely discharge it and the vocabulary gives no rule for choosing: Fz names the power, and Aw under law L16 names exactly this mechanic ('transfer-time enforcement where eligibility follows the holder'). Law L28 (Fz -> named authority + enumerated triggers + appeal path + holder disclosure) has one of four: the authority is named, the triggers, appeal and disclosure are not.
nodes.local_id: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F11

nodes.id: obligation:Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F12
nodes.label: F12 A named pauser role -- 0x1ac78dfcae082e9fe286d1ccb12c17a3e906b906 -- c
nodes.protocol: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets)
nodes.text: A named pauser role -- 0x1ac78dfcae082e9fe286d1ccb12c17a3e906b906 -- can halt all transfers of the token; paused() is currently false.
nodes.note: Gp is correct. As with WBTC, it does not distinguish a pause over all holders' transfers from a pause over new issuance.
nodes.local_id: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F12

nodes.id: obligation:Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F13
nodes.label: F13 The token's implementation can be replaced outright: cbBTC is a FiatTo
nodes.protocol: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets)
nodes.text: The token's implementation can be replaced outright: cbBTC is a FiatTokenProxy exposing upgradeTo, upgradeToAndCall and changeAdmin, currently pointing at FiatTokenV2_1 at 0x7458bfDC30034EB860B265E6068121D18Fa5Aa72 (solc 0.6.12), the same implementation address on Base and Ethereum, held in the legacy ZeppelinOS slot 0x7050c9e0... rather than the EIP-1967 slot, which reads zero.
nodes.note: Up is right and is the load-bearing difference between this entry and the other two custodial wrappers: nothing in WBTC or BTCB is comparable. Law L15 (Up -> Tg | bounded emergency process) is NOT satisfied -- see F14 -- and that failure is the finding, not a defect of the decomposition.
nodes.local_id: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F13

nodes.id: obligation:Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F14
nodes.label: F14 The holders of these powers are single keys: eth_getCode returns empty
nodes.protocol: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets)
nodes.text: The holders of these powers are single keys: eth_getCode returns empty for both owner and masterMinter, so there is no multisig contract and no timelock anywhere in the admin surface.
nodes.evidence: https://ethereum-rpc.publicnode.com eth_getCode(owner) and eth_getCode(masterMinter), both empty (accessed 2026-08-04)
nodes.note: RESIDUE, and the correction the corpus most needs. Giving Coinbase Up and withholding Tg gets the direction right for the wrong reason: it is not that the issuer chose upgradeability over delay, it is that there is no delay and no quorum at all. Prohibition X9 ('Up with immediate single-key control', class H) is precisely this shape and cannot be evaluated, because the vocabulary has no way to state that the holder of an element is one key -- and the holder type of the proxy admin specifically was not read on chain, so X9's antecedent remains unverified even for a human reader.
nodes.local_id: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F14

nodes.id: obligation:Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F15
nodes.label: F15 Authority is partitioned across keys: the owner can change owner, paus
nodes.protocol: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets)
nodes.text: Authority is partitioned across keys: the owner can change owner, pauser, blacklister, masterMinter and oracle, and cannot change the proxy owner, so upgrade authority sits behind a separate key from role administration.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. Control elements are unary predicates on a protocol; there is no way to state that two of them are held by different parties, which is the difference between one compromised key ending the system and one compromised key degrading it.
nodes.local_id: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F15

nodes.id: obligation:Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F16
nodes.label: F16 The contract that holds every balance is not the issuer's own code: th
nodes.protocol: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets)
nodes.text: The contract that holds every balance is not the issuer's own code: the repository states the token 'will be an exact duplicate of centre-tokens [FiatTokenV2_1]' and the proxy an exact duplicate of the centre-tokens proxy, and the issuer's repository has not been touched since 2023-05-12 and never mentions cbBTC or any of the newer wrapped assets by name.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. No element for provenance: that the security-relevant source is a third party's, that the issuer's own repository documents a different product, or that the repository declares MIT in package.json with no LICENSE file at the root. Byte-comparison against centre-tokens v2.1.0 was not performed.
nodes.local_id: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F16

nodes.id: obligation:Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F17
nodes.label: F17 The custodian of the underlying is also the largest venue on which the
nodes.protocol: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets)
nodes.text: The custodian of the underlying is also the largest venue on which the underlying trades, so the party whose failure would break the peg is the same party whose order book would price the break.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. A concentration property with direct depeg implications and no symbol; the nearest thing in the algebra is prohibition X3 (protocol token as collateral and oracle market and backstop), which is the same reflexivity worry stated only for a protocol's own token.
nodes.local_id: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F17

nodes.id: obligation:Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F18
nodes.label: F18 One reserve pool backs four networks' supply of cbBTC simultaneously (
nodes.protocol: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets)
nodes.text: One reserve pool backs four networks' supply of cbBTC simultaneously (48,338.78 Ethereum, 44,528.809, 3,108.551 and 78.272 on the others), reconciled only on the issuer's page.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. No element for a single reserve drawn against by several representations on different domains -- the same shape as BTCB's three representations. A per-chain supply is checkable, the aggregate against reserve is not, and only the aggregate is the peg.
nodes.local_id: Coinbase Bridge (cbBTC and other wrapped assets):F18

nodes.label: Hyperliquid Bridge
F1 A user transfers native Arbitrum USDC to the Bridge2 contract at 0x2Df
nodes.text: A user transfers native Arbitrum USDC to the Bridge2 contract at 0x2Df1c51E09aECF9cacB7bc98cB1742757f163dF7 and receives a credit to their Hyperliquid L1 account about a minute later; the contract holds $421,856,739.90 of native USDC plus $5,026.03 of legacy USDC.e.
nodes.note: SUPPLY-TOPOLOGY AXIS: lock-and-mint escrow on the source side, and the only entry of the five whose reserve is a first-class on-chain object -- law L9's debit is directly observable. RANKING BASIS, MIS-ATTRIBUTED: DefiLlama hyperliquid-bridge = $5,906,458,452 against the corpus's $5,893.6m, but it splits Arbitrum $421,919,062 / 'Hyperliquid L1' $5,484,539,389, and that second bucket is native USDC minted on Hyperliquid via Circle's CCTP which never touched this escrow. Roughly 93% of the ranked figure is canonical issuance, not bridge escrow. The rank ordering is unaffected; any claim of a '$5.9b bridge honeypot' is wrong by an order of magnitude. Decompose the system, not the number.

nodes.label: F2 A deposit is credited, and a withdrawal is authorised, only when valid
nodes.text: A deposit is credited, and a withdrawal is authorised, only when validators holding more than two thirds of staking power have signed it; there is no external verifier, no oracle and no third-party fraud proof.
nodes.note: Xm fires, and this is the strongest instance of it in the category -- an on-chain signature threshold against a set whose membership and weights are readable. VERIFICATION-MODEL AXIS: endogenous consensus, distinct from single-company attestation, from application-configured verifier sets, from a light client and from proof verification.

nodes.label: F3 The set that signs withdrawals is the same stake-weighted validator se
nodes.text: The set that signs withdrawals is the same stake-weighted validator set that secures the destination chain, so holding bridged funds adds no trust assumption beyond using Hyperliquid at all.
nodes.note: RESIDUE, and the single most important property of a native L1 bridge. Xm cannot express that the verifying set is endogenous. The consequence is that Xm assigned here and Xm assigned to a 1-of-1 external DVN configuration assert the same thing about opposite designs; prohibition X13 ('external-validator Xm securing value exceeding slashable stake') presumes an external set and cannot even classify this one.

nodes.label: F4 A deposit below the 5 USDC minimum is not credited and is lost permane
nodes.text: A deposit below the 5 USDC minimum is not credited and is lost permanently.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. No element for a minimum transfer size, and none for an irreversible loss on a malformed transfer. Small, but it is a hard economic term of the transfer that the construction cannot state.

nodes.label: F5 To withdraw, the user signs an EIP-712 WithdrawAction3 on Hyperliquid,
nodes.text: To withdraw, the user signs an EIP-712 WithdrawAction3 on Hyperliquid, the L1 balance is deducted immediately, validators sign, a request is posted to the Arbitrum contract, and a finalizer releases the USDC; funds arrive in three to four minutes.
nodes.note: The debit precedes the credit and is unconditional, which is the ordering that makes the dispute window (F6) a safety mechanism rather than a liquidity one.

nodes.label: F6 A posted withdrawal is released only after a 200-second dispute period
nodes.text: A posted withdrawal is released only after a 200-second dispute period, during which lockers may vote to lock the bridge and stop it; disputePeriodSeconds() = 200 and blockDurationMillis() = 350 are on-chain readable.
nodes.note: RESIDUE, and a CORPUS DEPARTURE: Wq is dropped from this obligation. The delay exists to give honest validators time to veto a fraudulent withdrawal, not to ration scarce liquidity among exiting claimants; Wq names the queue and misses the purpose entirely. Oa was also considered and rejected: there is no assertion, no bond and no adjudicator, only a veto window. A dispute window as a safety parameter has no symbol.

nodes.label: F7 The user pays a flat 1 USDC fee on Hyperliquid and never needs Arbitru
nodes.text: The user pays a flat 1 USDC fee on Hyperliquid and never needs Arbitrum ETH: the Arbitrum-side transaction that releases the funds is submitted and paid for by a finalizer.
nodes.note: CANDIDATE-REGISTER (Gs). A third party pays destination-domain gas and is compensated in the source domain's unit -- structurally the same behaviour as LayerZero's Executor, and the two together are the case for reading Gs cross-domain rather than only as an account-abstraction paymaster. Law L21 (Gs -> Au + metering + fee settlement) again fails on the Au term: the user grants nothing.

nodes.label: F8 Nothing is minted on the destination: what the user receives is a bala
nodes.text: Nothing is minted on the destination: what the user receives is a balance in HyperCore's ledger, not a transferable token, so there is no destination-side representation to hold, trade or bridge onward.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. SUPPLY-TOPOLOGY AXIS again, and none of the four topologies fits cleanly: it is escrow on one side and a ledger credit on the other. Xf presumes a transferable representation on the destination. There is also no mint or burn authority in the system at all, which is why no element from the issuance group appears in the construction.

nodes.label: F9 Two supplies of the same asset coexist on the destination chain with d
nodes.text: Two supplies of the same asset coexist on the destination chain with different trust models and are fungible to the user: $421.9m that came through this escrow and $5.48b issued natively on Hyperliquid via CCTP.
nodes.note: RESIDUE, and promoted from the corpus's residue-observation to a measurement: the ratio is 13:1 in favour of canonical issuance, so the escrow regime is now the minority one for its own asset on its own chain. No element for one asset carrying two trust models in one balance.

nodes.label: F10 The escrow has no owner and no upgrade path: implementation(), admin()
nodes.text: The escrow has no owner and no upgrade path: implementation(), admin() and owner() all revert, and every privileged action is authorised by validator signatures rather than by an admin key.
nodes.evidence: https://arbitrum-one-rpc.publicnode.com eth_call implementation(), admin(), owner() on Bridge2, all revert (accessed 2026-08-04) | https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hyperliquid-dex/contracts/master/Bridge2.sol (accessed 2026-08-04)
nodes.note: RESIDUE of the guarantee-by-absence kind. This is the only one of the five with no owning party, and the vocabulary can only say so by omitting Up, Tg and every holder -- which is indistinguishable from not having checked. It is the strongest control-plane fact in the category and the least expressible.

nodes.label: F11 Emergency powers are three, all held by the validator set: lockers vot
nodes.text: Emergency powers are three, all held by the validator set: lockers vote to trigger an emergency lock which pauses the contract, invalidateWithdrawals cancels pending withdrawals under a cold-wallet quorum, and emergencyUnlock requires cold-wallet signatures of two thirds of stake and installs a new validator set; paused() is currently false.
nodes.note: APPROXIMATE. Gp names the pause facility and nothing else: not that the power is exercised by a vote of the same principals who authorise ordinary flow, not that a cold-key quorum can cancel already-authorised withdrawals, and not that the emergency exit re-seats the authority itself. A cold-wallet lock is a different emergency posture from a contract pause and the corpus already flags that gap.

nodes.label: F12 The same principals hold two key tiers with different powers: hot keys
nodes.text: The same principals hold two key tiers with different powers: hot keys sign routine deposits and withdrawals, cold keys invalidate withdrawals and re-seat the validator set; hotValidatorSetHash() and coldValidatorSetHash() are distinct on-chain state.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. No vocabulary for 'the same principals, two escalation tiers'. This is the holder problem in its most refined form: not who holds the power, but which of a single party's key sets holds which power.

nodes.label: F13 Two named roles exist that are neither owners nor governance: lockers,
nodes.text: Two named roles exist that are neither owners nor governance: lockers, who can vote the bridge into a lock, and finalizers, who submit the transaction that releases a withdrawal after the dispute period.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. The control group knows owners, guardians, timelocks and proxies; it has no way to name an operational role with one specific privileged action and no ownership.

nodes.label: F14 The verifier set is maintained by a staking lifecycle: HYPE is delegat
nodes.text: The verifier set is maintained by a staking lifecycle: HYPE is delegated to validators, each validator must self-delegate 10,000 HYPE locked for a year, delegations carry a one-day lockup, and unresponsive validators are jailed by peer vote; 34 validators exist, 27 are active, and 436,005,726 HYPE is staked.
nodes.note: CANDIDATE-REGISTER (Vl). A firm fit for the lifecycle itself -- delegation, bonding, jailing, rotation -- with the caveat that the lifecycle belongs to the L1 and the bridge merely reads its output. Note that Vl's usual companion Bs is absent here, which the vocabulary treats as unremarkable and F16 shows is the whole story.

nodes.label: F15 Moving HYPE from a staking account to a spot account goes through a se
nodes.text: Moving HYPE from a staking account to a spot account goes through a seven-day unstaking queue, with at most five withdrawals pending at once.
nodes.note: RE-SITING of the corpus's Wq. The corpus assigned Wq to the bridge's 200-second dispute window, where it is wrong (F6); the genuine Wq-shaped object in this system is this queue -- a delay with a concurrency cap on exits from the capital that constitutes the verifier set. Scope caveat: it belongs to staking rather than to the escrow, and is included because the verifier set's exit dynamics are what the bridge depends on.

nodes.label: F16 Validator stake is not slashable: the documentation states that there
nodes.text: Validator stake is not slashable: the documentation states that there is currently no automatic slashing implemented, so the only consequences for a validator are jailing by peer vote and the seven-day queue, and no path exists from a bridge failure to a loss of stake.
nodes.note: RESIDUE, and a CORPUS DEPARTURE: Bs is dropped outright. Bs means slashable first-loss capital and there is none to slash -- worse than the corpus's marker, which says only that the stake is not posted specifically as bridge collateral. What exists is stake as control value and reputation with no loss path, and that has no symbol. Consequence for the algebra: prohibition X13 compares secured value against slashable stake, and with slashable stake at zero the comparison is degenerate on the one protocol in this category it was written for.

nodes.label: F17 The two-thirds threshold is evaluated over a concentrated distribution
nodes.text: The two-thirds threshold is evaluated over a concentrated distribution: five Hyper Foundation validators hold 212,971,320 of 436,005,726 HYPE, or 48.85%, so one operator family is far above the one third needed to veto any withdrawal or validator-set update and needs only a further sixth of stake to act alone.
nodes.note: RESIDUE, and the sharpest instance of the holder problem in the category: the element (Xm) records that a threshold exists, and the security is entirely a property of the distribution behind it, which no element carries. A 2/3 rule over a 48.85% bloc is a different mechanism from a 2/3 rule over an even distribution, and the two decompose identically.

nodes.label: F18 Validator-set updates are themselves subject to the dispute period and
nodes.text: Validator-set updates are themselves subject to the dispute period and are ordered by an on-chain epoch counter, epoch() = 7.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. Ep was considered and rejected: the counter orders authority rotations and prevents replay of stale set updates rather than gating a transition on an epoch boundary. The mechanism -- the authority that can change the authority is subject to the same delay as ordinary flow -- is a real safety property with no name.

nodes.label: F19 No reserve attestation exists or is needed: the escrow is a contract b
nodes.text: No reserve attestation exists or is needed: the escrow is a contract balance that anyone can read directly, and the issuer publishes nothing about it.
nodes.note: RESIDUE of the discharge-by-construction kind, which the options lane raised as a formalism-level gap: the obligation that At exists to discharge cannot arise here, and the requirement language admits only discharge by naming a satisfying element. Omitting At therefore reads as 'no attestation' -- the same string a decomposition of an unaudited custodian would produce -- when the correct reading is 'attestation is unnecessary because the reserve is a first-class on-chain object'. Two opposite epistemic states, one representation.

nodes.label: LayerZero V2
F1 A packet sent from a source contract through the immutable EndpointV2
nodes.text: A packet sent from a source contract through the immutable EndpointV2 is delivered exactly once to a named destination contract on a named remote endpoint, under a per-pathway nonce that binds the message to its channel and prevents replay; the Ethereum endpoint is 0x1a44076050125825900e736c501f859c50fe728c with eid 30101.
nodes.note: This is the part of law L18 (Xm -> explicit finality + chain/domain binding + replay protection) that the protocol genuinely discharges: domain binding by eid and replay protection by nonce. LayerZero is not a bridge; it is the messaging layer bridges are built on, so its obligations are conditional on an application supplying the asset half.

nodes.label: F2 A delivered packet is accepted only after every required Decentralized
nodes.text: A delivered packet is accepted only after every required Decentralized Verifier Network has attested to the same payloadHash and enough optional DVNs have attested to meet a threshold -- the X-of-Y-of-N security stack -- configured per application, per remote endpoint and per direction.
nodes.note: APPROXIMATE, and the most over-loaded use of Xm anywhere in this category. Xm asserts 'messages are verified' and carries none of: who verifies, how many, whether the set is chosen by the application or by the protocol, and what happens when the set is one party. VERIFICATION-MODEL AXIS: application-configured verifier sets -- distinct from single-company attestation (WBTC, Coinbase, BTCB, CCTP), from endogenous consensus (Hyperliquid), from a light client, and from proof verification, none of which the top five use.

nodes.label: F3 Verification security is a per-application parameter rather than a pro
nodes.text: Verification security is a per-application parameter rather than a protocol property: two applications on the same endpoint pair can run entirely different verifier sets and thresholds, and one of them may be a single company.
nodes.note: RESIDUE, and the #2 entry's defining feature is invisible in the vocabulary. A decomposition that gives LayerZero Xm says the same thing about a 1-of-1 configuration and a 5-of-9 one. The element is a unary predicate on a protocol where the property being asserted belongs to a configuration held by a third party.

nodes.label: F4 An application that does not set its configuration inherits protocol d
nodes.text: An application that does not set its configuration inherits protocol defaults, which the documentation warns are placeholders that 'may be Dead DVNs that prevent message delivery' -- a Dead DVN is deployed on each chain, 0x747c741496a507e4b404b50463e691a8d692f6ac on Ethereum -- while the historical default in the other direction was a 1-of-1 LayerZero Labs DVN.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. Inherited security -- the security an application gets when it specifies nothing -- is a mechanism with two opposite failure modes (a bricked pathway or an unguarded one) and no symbol. Kelp's position that 1-of-1 was the documented default, with roughly 40% of protocols on it, is a party's claim, not a first-party page; LayerZero's own statement that it 'made a mistake' in allowing its verifier network to secure high-value assets in that configuration is reported by the same outlet. Its post-mortem page was not locatable on layerzero.network/blog.

nodes.label: F5 Safety on a pathway is exactly the honesty of the configured verifier
nodes.text: Safety on a pathway is exactly the honesty of the configured verifier set: on 2026-04-18, with rsETH configured to a single verifier -- the LayerZero Labs DVN -- and two LayerZero-hosted RPC nodes compromised, approximately $292m / 116,500 rsETH was minted on a destination without a matching source burn.
nodes.note: RESIDUE, and the strongest empirical support available for the corpus's own claim that Xm conflates verification models: it converts the argument into a measurement. The corpus carries no record of the exploit. Prohibition X7 ('cross-domain mint whose verifier is present but unproven correct', class H) is the nearest rule and it fires on every entry in this category equally, so it does not separate a 1-of-1 from a 5-of-9 either.

nodes.label: F6 An Executor watches for sufficient verification, commits the nonce, ca
nodes.text: An Executor watches for sufficient verification, commits the nonce, calls lzReceive on the destination and fronts the destination-chain gas on the sender's behalf, recovering it from the fee quoted and paid on the source chain; on Ethereum the Executor is 0x173272739bd7aa6e4e214714048a9fe699453059.
nodes.note: CANDIDATE-REGISTER (Gs). Genuinely a sponsored-fee liability: a third party pays gas in one domain's unit and is repaid in another's. Gs is written for account-abstraction paymasters, so law L21 (Gs -> Au + metering + fee settlement) reads oddly here -- there is fee settlement and metering by quote, but no user-granted Au. The same candidate covers Hyperliquid's finalizer, which is evidence for promoting it out of the candidate register with a cross-domain reading added.

nodes.label: F7 Safety and liveness are held by two different role types: DVNs decide
nodes.text: Safety and liveness are held by two different role types: DVNs decide whether a message is true, Executors decide whether it arrives, and the loss of each has a different consequence -- a corrupted DVN set mints falsely, an absent Executor merely stalls.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. The separation is the design; Xm collapses it and Gs names only the paying half. Nothing in the vocabulary distinguishes a role whose failure is a safety failure from one whose failure is a liveness failure.

nodes.label: F8 Under the OFT standard, tokens are burned on the source chain and mint
nodes.text: Under the OFT standard, tokens are burned on the source chain and minted on the destination, so total supply across all chains is conserved, no escrow exists, and an exploit cannot exceed what was burned.
nodes.note: SUPPLY-TOPOLOGY AXIS, first of two the same protocol supports: burn-and-mint canonical-style issuance under an application's own token.

nodes.label: F9 Under the OFT Adapter, the original token is locked in a lockbox contr
nodes.text: Under the OFT Adapter, the original token is locked in a lockbox contract on its home chain and a representation circulates elsewhere, concentrating value in an escrow.
nodes.note: SUPPLY-TOPOLOGY AXIS, second: lock-and-mint escrow. RANKING BASIS: DefiLlama layerzero = $6,669,281,380 against the corpus's $6,666.7m, of which $6,374,017,781 is Ethereum alone -- the measured TVL is almost entirely this adapter leg, because the burn-and-mint leg contributes no TVL by construction. Rank #2 stands, but the number measures one of the protocol's two topologies and is blind to the other, which is the same blindness that keeps CCTP off the list entirely.

nodes.label: F10 The two topologies have opposite attack surfaces and the same user-vis
nodes.text: The two topologies have opposite attack surfaces and the same user-visible interface, so the question 'how much can be stolen' has a different answer per token on one protocol.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. Both are Xf. The corpus names this gap and it is confirmed here at the sharpest possible site: not two protocols with one symbol, but one protocol whose two modes have one symbol.

nodes.label: F11 Mint and burn authority, and custody of any lockbox, belong to the app
nodes.text: Mint and burn authority, and custody of any lockbox, belong to the application's own contract and its owner, not to LayerZero, so the party that must be trusted for supply conservation is one the protocol does not name.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. Containment between protocols again: the trust question moves from the decomposed protocol to an application the decomposition cannot reference. The carrier composes peers by union of element sets and has no relation for 'A's safety is a property of B'.

nodes.label: F12 The Endpoint's code cannot be replaced -- 24,005 bytes of direct non-p
nodes.text: The Endpoint's code cannot be replaced -- 24,005 bytes of direct non-proxy bytecode, documented as immutable and permissionless -- and it is nevertheless owned: owner() = 0xbe010a7e3686fdf65e93344ab664d065a0b02478, a custom multisig with threshold() = 3 and nonce() = 611, carrying no secondsTimeLocked and no getMinDelay.
nodes.evidence: https://ethereum-rpc.publicnode.com eth_call EndpointV2.owner(), eth_getCode (24,005 bytes, no implementation slot), owner threshold() = 3, secondsTimeLocked()/getMinDelay() absent (accessed 2026-08-04) | https://docs.layerzero.network/v2/home/protocol/protocol-overview (accessed 2026-08-04)
nodes.note: RESIDUE, and two CORPUS DEPARTURES. Up is dropped: EndpointV2 is not a proxy and has no implementation slot, so the corpus symbol captures the right worry ('the protocol can change under you') with the wrong mechanism. Tg is dropped: the owner executes immediately on a 3-signature quorum, the same error the corpus makes on WBTC. An immutable contract that is nonetheless owned has no name -- and once again the missing information is the holder: a 3-of-n, not a delay and not a proxy.

nodes.label: F13 There is no protocol-level pause: paused() and pause() both revert on
nodes.text: There is no protocol-level pause: paused() and pause() both revert on EndpointV2, so no party can stop message flow by pausing the endpoint.
nodes.evidence: https://ethereum-rpc.publicnode.com eth_call EndpointV2.paused() and pause(), both revert (accessed 2026-08-04)
nodes.note: CORPUS DEPARTURE: Gp is dropped. A guardian pause may exist per-OApp, but that is the application's power, not the protocol's, and the decomposition is of the protocol. Same guarantee-by-absence problem as WBTC F13: the vocabulary cannot assert that a power does not exist.

nodes.label: F14 The Endpoint owner controls which message libraries are registered --
nodes.text: The Endpoint owner controls which message libraries are registered -- getRegisteredLibraries() returns 4 entries, including a blockedLibrary at 0x1ccbf0db9c192d969de57e25b3ff09a25bb1d862 -- and the protocol-level defaults, so delivery on a pathway can be stopped or redirected by configuration.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. Gp was considered and rejected: the effect resembles a pause but the mechanism is a registry swap with no pause semantics, no emergency trigger and no scope limit. This is the mutable surface of an immutable contract and the reason F12's 'immutable' is a claim about code and not about behaviour.

nodes.label: F15 An application's send and receive configuration -- its verifier set, i
nodes.text: An application's send and receive configuration -- its verifier set, its threshold and its libraries -- can be changed at any time by the application's owner, with no delay and no notice, including while messages are in flight.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. Tg names delay in changing code or parameters and there is none; Up names mutable code and this is mutable security parameters. Mutability of the security stack is the specific power that makes F3 dangerous, and it has no symbol.

nodes.label: F16 An application owner may name a delegate authorised to set that config
nodes.text: An application owner may name a delegate authorised to set that configuration on the application's behalf, revocably.
nodes.note: APPROXIMATE. Au ('delegated execution scope') names the relation -- a named party may act within a bounded scope and be revoked -- but is written for user-side session policy, and law L17 (Au -> bounded scope + revocation + expiry + nonce/domain separation) will not be satisfied: the delegate has scope and revocation, no expiry and no nonce discipline. Recorded as an approximate fit rather than residue because the delegation relation is exactly what the symbol names; the mis-fit is that the delegator is an admin rather than a user, which is the holder problem in yet another place.

nodes.label: F17 Fees may optionally be denominated in a protocol token, and this is a
nodes.text: Fees may optionally be denominated in a protocol token, and this is a per-chain parameter: lzToken() is address(0) on Ethereum, so ZRO fee payment is not enabled there while it is elsewhere.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. Minor, but it is one more parameter of the protocol that differs per deployment, and the vocabulary has no way to say that an element is instantiated differently on each of 180 mainnet deployments.

nodes.label: F18 A received message can itself trigger further cross-domain calls throu
nodes.text: A received message can itself trigger further cross-domain calls through lzCompose, so a transfer composes horizontally into a sequence of domain-crossing actions.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. Xf and Xm each describe one hop. Nothing names a composed multi-hop action whose intermediate states are on different domains -- the same shape as the hub-and-spoke two-hop routing the corpus flags for USDT0.

nodes.label: WBTC
F1 A holder's bitcoin is taken into the custody of a named off-chain lega
nodes.text: A holder's bitcoin is taken into the custody of a named off-chain legal entity, and the equality of one WBTC to one BTC rests entirely on that entity continuing to hold, and to honour claims against, the bitcoin; no Ethereum contract holds, references or can reach the bitcoin.
nodes.note: RESIDUE, and the category headline: what secures the peg is a company's promise, and no element of the 58 names custody by an off-chain legal entity. Note that law L8 ('Xf -> Xm | named custodian, plus a global claim ledger') anticipates exactly this case and discharges it by a 'named custodian' that is not itself an element -- the law's own alternative branch lies outside the algebra, so a construction can satisfy L8 with something the vocabulary cannot write down. Custody now spans three jurisdictions (BiT Global holds the user and backup keys in Hong Kong and Singapore, BitGo retains one of three keys via a US entity), so recourse is a three-jurisdiction question; the corpus residue still says 'BitGo holds bitcoin'.

nodes.label: F2 WBTC is minted on Ethereum in the amount of bitcoin received at the cu
nodes.text: WBTC is minted on Ethereum in the amount of bitcoin received at the custodian deposit address, so a claim in the Bitcoin domain becomes a spendable ERC-20 claim in the Ethereum domain; on-chain supply is 116,132.18273272 WBTC.
nodes.note: Xf is the only element that fires anywhere in this system's cross-domain behaviour. Law L9 (debit(source) = credit(destination)) is stated over two ledgers the construction cannot relate: the Bitcoin-side debit is observable but the binding between it and the Ethereum-side credit is an off-chain assertion by one party.

nodes.label: F3 Nothing on Ethereum verifies that the Bitcoin deposit occurred: Factor
nodes.text: Nothing on Ethereum verifies that the Bitcoin deposit occurred: Factory.confirmMintRequest() is gated by onlyCustodian, resolving through Controller.isCustodian() to the single address 0xb0f42d187145911c2ad1755831aded125619bd27, and the custodian's confirmation transaction is itself the bridge.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. Xm is explicitly NOT discharged and must not be assigned: there is no message, no proof, no light client, no verifier set and no threshold. Stronger than 'absent': on this domain pair no verification element is constructible at all, because Bitcoin cannot execute verification code -- the vocabulary's cross-domain group assumes two programmable domains. VERIFICATION-MODEL AXIS: single-company attestation, and the weakest instance of it, since the attestation is a transaction rather than a signed statement about reserves.

nodes.label: F4 No contract escrows the underlying: the backing is a set of 20 Bitcoin
nodes.text: No contract escrows the underlying: the backing is a set of 20 Bitcoin addresses published by the issuer, so there is no on-chain object whose balance constitutes the reserve.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. SUPPLY-TOPOLOGY AXIS: custodial wrap, not lock-and-mint escrow, not burn-and-mint canonical issuance, not liquidity-network fill. Xf is common to all four and separates none of them; the difference decides whether an exploit is bounded by the burned amount, by an escrow balance, or by a legal promise. Contrast Hyperliquid, where the reserve is a first-class on-chain object.

nodes.label: F5 Only an address in the on-chain merchant registry may request a mint o
nodes.text: Only an address in the on-chain merchant registry may request a mint or execute a burn, and only the registered custodian may confirm or reject it; Members.getMerchants() returns 47 addresses today.
nodes.note: Aw is a firm fit here and only here among the three custodial wrappers: an on-chain registry of principals with role-gated entry, not an owner check. It is issuer-side rather than user-side -- ordinary holders face no gate -- which is the same qualification the corpus attached to Aw for CCTP.

nodes.label: F6 Before submitting a mint request the merchant performs KYC/AML on the
nodes.text: Before submitting a mint request the merchant performs KYC/AML on the requester, so entry to the system is conditioned on an identity check performed by a firm that the contracts never observe.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. Aw names an enforced on-chain gate; this is diligence performed off-chain by an intermediating principal whose performance is unobservable and unfalsifiable on chain. No element names an intermediating principal at all -- the merchant is simultaneously a gatekeeper, the only party who may transact with the Factory, and a bilateral fee-taker.

nodes.label: F7 A merchant approves the Factory for its WBTC, calls burn(), and the cu
nodes.text: A merchant approves the Factory for its WBTC, calls burn(), and the custodian sends BTC to that merchant's registered Bitcoin address after 25 Ethereum confirmations.
nodes.note: APPROXIMATE. Rd asserts that a direct redemption right exists and is silent on who holds it. Here it is held by 47 firms and by nobody else, so the symbol is true of the system and false of essentially every holder. Ps was considered and rejected: there is no on-chain module holding a reserve to swap 1:1 against.

nodes.label: F8 An ordinary WBTC holder has no contract-enforced way to obtain BTC and
nodes.text: An ordinary WBTC holder has no contract-enforced way to obtain BTC and exits only by selling into a secondary market.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. No element for a redemption right vested in a party other than the token holder, nor for redemption friction (who may redeem, on what timeline, at what minimum size), which is what actually determines whether the peg holds under stress.

nodes.label: F9 The issuer publishes a live proof-of-reserve listing every custodian a
nodes.text: The issuer publishes a live proof-of-reserve listing every custodian address and its balance -- 116,514.34 BTC against 116,499.20 WBTC across 20 addresses -- and third parties consume that listing as the protocol's reserve, DefiLlama's adapter reading the same audit page.
nodes.note: APPROXIMATE. Law L27 requires of At a named attester, independence, a stated assurance level, a staleness bound and recourse. This has an issuer, a refresh, and none of the other four. At cannot distinguish 'here are 20 addresses, check them yourself' from 'an auditor signed a report last quarter', and that difference is the entire epistemic content. RANKING BASIS: DefiLlama wbtc = $7,314,780,495 on 2026-08-04 against the corpus's $7,300.5m, hours apart; rank #1 stands and the figure is the sum of the balances of the addresses the issuer itself publishes. WITHDRAWN: L27 requires of At a named attester, independence, a stated assurance level, a staleness bound and recourse. The cited disclosure is published by the issuer and supplies none of the last four, so At is not discharged and this obligation is residue.

nodes.label: F10 Anyone can verify the balances of the 20 published addresses; nobody c
nodes.text: Anyone can verify the balances of the 20 published addresses; nobody can verify that those addresses belong to the custodian, that the bitcoin in them is unencumbered, or that it is not rehypothecated.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. The address-to-custodian mapping is an assertion, not a proof. No element separates the checkable half of a reserve claim from the unfalsifiable half.

nodes.label: F11 The custodian mints only after six Bitcoin confirmations and pays out
nodes.text: The custodian mints only after six Bitcoin confirmations and pays out only after 25 Ethereum confirmations, which is the design's entire treatment of source-domain finality and reorg exposure.
nodes.note: RESIDUE. No element for source-chain finality or reorg exposure -- named in the corpus's own categoryResidue and unfilled. Ep was considered and rejected: these are confirmation depths applied off-chain by one party, not an on-chain epoch boundary gating a transition.

nodes.label: F12 The Controller's owner can pause and unpause all WBTC transfers; pause
nodes.text: The Controller's owner can pause and unpause all WBTC transfers; paused() is currently false.
